subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Development Time After First Crack
description: One-minute skill: Development Time After First Crack.

hook.text: Development time is how long the roast continues after first crack. It's measured in both seconds and percentage.

buildup.text: Short development (under 15% of total roast) keeps bright acids and fruit notes. Long development deepens body and sweetness.

discovery.text: Under-developed coffee tastes grassy, sour, and thin. Over-developed tastes flat, ashy, and bitter.

twist.text: The ideal development zone is surprisingly narrow—often just 30–60 seconds. Seconds matter enormously at this stage.

climax.text: Experienced roasters develop an intuitive feel for this window through smell, sound, color, and bean temperature data.

punchline.text: Too short, it's sour. Too long, it's flat. The sweet spot lasts seconds.

quiz.question: What happens when coffee is under-developed after first crack?
options: It tastes grassy, sour, and thin

details.summary: Development time is the period between first crack and the end of the roast. It determines how fully the bean's sugars caramelize and flavors mature. Too short a development yields sour, grassy notes; too long produces flat, baked flavors.
details.whyItMatters: Development time is the most common variable roasters adjust to fine-tune flavor. Even a few seconds can shift a coffee from bright and fruity to sweet and chocolatey.
takeaways: Development time runs from first crack to the roast's end
Short development preserves acidity but risks sourness
Long development adds sweetness but can flatten complexity

faq.question: What is a typical development time ratio for specialty roasts?
faq.answer: Many specialty roasters target a development time ratio of 20 to 25 percent of total roast time. For a twelve-minute roast, that means roughly two and a half to three minutes after first crack.

faq.question: How does development time affect espresso versus filter brewing?
faq.answer: Espresso benefits from slightly longer development that increases solubility and sweetness under pressure. Filter brewing favors shorter development to preserve acidity and aromatic complexity.
